title: The Fair Games Theorem
description: In a fair game (expected gain is zero), a gambler with finite wealth playing against an infinitely wealthy opponent will eventually go bankrupt with probability 1.

overview.historicalContext: The Fair Games Theorem (Optional Stopping Theorem) originates in the development of martingale theory during the early-to-mid 20th century. In 1906 Louis Bachelier applied fair-game reasoning to model financial markets in his Theorie de la speculation. Paul Levy formalized the concept of conditional expectation sequences in the 1930s, and in 1939 Jean Ville introduced the term 'martingale' (borrowed from a doubling betting strategy). The decisive advance came in 1953 when Joseph Doob proved the Optional Stopping Theorem as part of his comprehensive treatment of martingale theory in 'Stochastic Processes'. Doob showed that for any martingale X and bounded stopping time tau, E[X_tau] = E[X_0], rigorously establishing that no strategy can beat a fair game. This result became Wiedijk's #62 in his list of 100 greatest theorems, and it remains foundational for modern probability, mathematical finance (via the Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing), and statistical sequential analysis.
overview.problemStatement: The Fair Games Theorem (Wiedijk #62, also known as the Optional Stopping Theorem) states: if X is a martingale with respect to a filtration F and tau, pi are bounded stopping times with tau <= pi, then E[X_tau] = E[X_pi]. In particular, E[X_tau] = E[X_0] for any bounded stopping time tau. Informally, no betting strategy based only on observed outcomes can change the expected value of a fair game.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization proves E[f_tau] = E[f_pi] by exploiting the fact that a martingale is simultaneously a submartingale and a supermartingale. From the submartingale property, Mathlib's expected_stoppedValue_mono gives E[f_tau] <= E[f_pi]. From the supermartingale property (by negating to get a submartingale of -f), we obtain E[f_tau] >= E[f_pi]. Applying le_antisymm yields the equality. The corollary E[f_tau] = E[f_0] follows by setting tau_0 = 0 (a trivially bounded stopping time). An iff-characterization shows that stopped-value monotonicity is equivalent to the submartingale property.
keyInsights: A martingale is both a submartingale and supermartingale; applying the stopped-value inequality in both directions and using le_antisymm gives equality E[f_tau] = E[f_pi]
The key Mathlib lemma is Submartingale.expected_stoppedValue_mono, which provides the one-sided inequality; the proof negates f to obtain the reverse inequality from the supermartingale
Boundedness of the stopping time (tau <= N) is essential: without it, strategies like 'play until you win' could violate the conclusion
The submartingale_iff_expected_stoppedValue_mono characterization connects the local conditional-expectation property to the global stopped-value monotonicity
Applications span gambling (gambler's ruin, failure of betting systems), finance (risk-neutral pricing, American options), and statistics (sequential testing, Wald's equation)

sections.title: Part I: Martingale Definitions
sections.summary: Defines isFairGame as a wrapper around Mathlib's MeasureTheory.Martingale, interpreting the martingale property as a fair game where E[f_{n+1} | F_n] = f_n. Includes fair_coin_flip_martingale_property as a placeholder illustrating that cumulative sums of fair flips form a martingale.

sections.title: Part II: Stopping Times
sections.summary: Defines isValidStoppingStrategy wrapping Mathlib's IsStoppingTime, and isBoundedStoppingTime requiring tau(omega) <= N for all omega. Also defines stoppedValue' computing X(tau(omega), omega), the value of the process when the gambler quits.

sections.title: Part III: The Fair Games Theorem (Optional Stopping)
sections.summary: Contains the main theorem fair_games_theorem proving E[f_tau] = E[f_pi] for bounded stopping times tau <= pi of a martingale f. The proof uses le_antisymm: the submartingale direction gives <=, and negating f to exploit the supermartingale direction gives >=. Includes fair_games_corollary (E[f_tau] = E[f_0]) and fair_games_theorem_stoppedValue using Mathlib's stoppedValue notation.

sections.title: Part IV: Characterization via Optional Stopping
sections.summary: States the axiom submartingale_of_stoppedValue_mono (converse direction of the iff characterization) and proves submartingale_characterization: a process is a submartingale iff stopped values are monotone for all bounded stopping times. The martingale_equality_characterization lifts this to equality for martingales.

sections.title: Part V: Applications
sections.summary: Presents four application statements as True-valued theorems with extensive doc comments: gambler's ruin probability P(success) = W_0/(W_0+a), failure of betting systems (martingale, D'Alembert, Fibonacci), option pricing under risk-neutral measures, and Doob's maximal inequality P(max f_n >= lambda) <= E[f_N]/lambda.

sections.title: Part VI: Why Fair Games Theorem (Wiedijk #62)
sections.summary: Summarizes the theorem's place in Wiedijk's 100 Greatest Theorems list, its historical significance for probability theory, gambling, and finance, and the three connected ideas of fairness (martingale), strategy (stopping time), and invariance (theorem). Concludes with fair_games_summary.

conclusion.summary: The Fair Games Theorem (Wiedijk #62) is formalized by proving that for any martingale f and bounded stopping times tau <= pi, the expectations E[f_tau] = E[f_pi] are equal. The proof leverages the dual sub/supermartingale nature of martingales and Mathlib's optional stopping inequality. This rigorously establishes that no strategy based on observed information can improve expected outcomes in a fair game.
conclusion.implications: The theorem is foundational across multiple domains. In gambling theory it explains gambler's ruin and why all betting systems (martingale doubling, D'Alembert, Fibonacci) fail against bounded play. In mathematical finance it underpins the Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing: discounted prices are martingales under the risk-neutral measure, so fair option pricing follows from optional stopping. In statistics it grounds Wald's sequential probability ratio test and sequential analysis. Doob's maximal inequality, a cornerstone of stochastic process theory, follows from optional stopping arguments.
openQuestions: What are the precise conditions under which the optional stopping theorem extends to unbounded stopping times (e.g., uniformly integrable martingales)?
How does the theorem generalize to continuous-time martingales and Brownian motion, where the bounded stopping time condition becomes more subtle?
What is the exact distribution of ruin times in the gambler's ruin problem, and how does it relate to first-passage times of random walks?
Can the submartingale characterization via stopped values be extended to more general index sets (e.g., continuous-time filtrations)?
